sections.skill: Track a running balance and read a bank statement

questions.prompt: Nina starts with $215.60 in checking. She deposits $84.25, buys shoes for $59.99, and pays a $42.00 bill. What is her balance?
questions.intro: An account register (or a budgeting app) records every transaction and keeps a running balance. Add each deposit (money in). Subtract each withdrawal, payment, or purchase (money out). Recording each item as it happens shows what you truly have.

misconceptions.D: Adds the purchases instead of subtracting
misconceptions.A: Subtracts the deposit instead of adding

sources: CFPB (Regulation E, 12 CFR 1005.6): Report unauthorized electronic transfers within 60 days after the statement showing them is sent; after that, liability can be unlimited for later transfers that timely notice would have prevented. (https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1005/6/)

questions.prompt: A bank statement shows: beginning balance $640.00; total deposits $1,120.00; total withdrawals $1,395.50. What is the ending balance?
questions.intro: A bank statement summarizes one period, usually a month: the balance at the start, every deposit and withdrawal, any fees or interest, and the balance at the end. Ending balance = beginning balance + deposits − withdrawals.

misconceptions.D: Adds the withdrawals instead of subtracting
misconceptions.A: Subtracts withdrawals from deposits but leaves out the beginning balance
misconceptions.C: Adds the beginning balance to withdrawals and subtracts deposits

sources: CFPB (Regulation E, 12 CFR 1005.6): Report unauthorized electronic transfers within 60 days after the statement showing them is sent; after that, liability can be unlimited for later transfers that timely notice would have prevented. questions.prompt: A statement shows a beginning balance of $410.00, withdrawals of $760.00, and an ending balance of $300.00. What were the total deposits?
questions.intro: The statement equation (beginning + deposits − withdrawals = ending) can be used to find any missing amount. Substitute what you know and solve for the unknown.

misconceptions.B: Subtracts instead of solving for the missing amount

sources: CFPB (Regulation E, 12 CFR 1005.6): Report unauthorized electronic transfers within 60 days after the statement showing them is sent; after that, liability can be unlimited for later transfers that timely notice would have prevented. questions.prompt: Carlos's balance is $42.10. A $55.00 automatic payment goes through anyway. What does his account show afterward?
questions.intro: If more money leaves an account than it holds, the balance becomes negative: the account is "overdrawn." A negative balance is money owed to the bank, often with a fee added. It must be repaid by depositing money.
questions.feedback: $42.10 − $55.00 = −$12.90. Carlos owes the bank $12.90, plus any overdraft fee.

misconceptions.C: Ignores the sign; thinks the account still has money
misconceptions.B: Thinks a balance cannot go below zero

questions.prompt: Ivy wrote a $75 check to her landlord on May 30. Her May 31 bank statement does not show it. Why?

choices.text: The landlord had not yet deposited the check when the statement closed
The bank forgot to charge the check, so Ivy gets to keep the $75
Checks never appear on bank statements
The check was paid from Ivy's savings account automatically

questions.correct_answer: The landlord had not yet deposited the check when the statement closed
questions.intro: A check you write is paid only when the person you paid deposits or cashes it, which can take days or weeks. Until then, the money is still in your account, but it is already promised.
questions.feedback: An "outstanding" check has been written but not yet cashed. It will appear later, so Ivy's register must still subtract it.

misconceptions.B: Thinks a missing item means the payment is cancelled

sections.relationship: Running-balance and statement problems require knowing which transactions add and which subtract.

questions.prompt: Which transaction INCREASES a checking account balance?

choices.text: A paycheck deposited by direct deposit
A debit card purchase at a store
An ATM cash withdrawal
An automatic payment for this month's phone bill

questions.correct_answer: A paycheck deposited by direct deposit
questions.intro: Money coming into an account (deposits, direct deposits, transfers in, interest) is a credit and increases the balance. Money going out (purchases, withdrawals, bill payments, fees) is a debit and decreases it.
questions.feedback: A deposit is money in; the other three are money out.
sources: CFPB (Regulation E, 12 CFR 1005.6): Report unauthorized electronic transfers within 60 days after the statement showing them is sent; after that, liability can be unlimited for later transfers that timely notice would have prevented. (https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1005/6/)

questions.prompt: On a bank statement, which item is a debit?

choices.text: $0.42 of interest earned
A $200 transfer in from savings
A $50 refund from a store
A $3.00 ATM fee

questions.intro: On a bank statement, "debit" means money taken out of the account, and "credit" means money added. Fees are debits; interest earned and refunds are credits.
questions.feedback: The fee is taken from the account, so it is a debit.

misconceptions.B: Thinks a transfer in is money out
misconceptions.C: Thinks a refund is money out

choices.text: It goes down to $90
It goes up to $150
It stays at $120 until the end of the month
It goes down to $30

questions.intro: Each purchase with a debit card lowers your balance by the purchase amount.

misconceptions.C: Thinks purchases wait until month end
misconceptions.D: Confuses the price with the new balance

questions.prompt: Why should you record a purchase in your register right away?

choices.text: Because the bank charges a fee each month if you do not record it
Because unrecorded purchases are free
Because the store needs a copy of your register
So your balance shows what you really have left to spend

questions.correct_answer: So your balance shows what you really have left to spend
questions.feedback: Recording each item immediately keeps your running balance accurate.

misconceptions.B: Thinks unrecorded items are not charged

choices.text: A check you wrote, a bill payment, and a monthly fee
A deposit, a check you wrote, and a refund

A paycheck, a gift deposited, and interest

questions.correct_answer: A check you wrote, a bill payment, and a monthly fee
questions.feedback: Checks you write, bill payments, and fees are all money out.

questions.prompt: Sam's statement ending balance is $520. He has a $150 deposit the bank had not received yet and two outstanding checks of $60 and $45. What is his adjusted (true) balance?
questions.intro: Reconciling means checking that your records match the bank's. Start with the statement's ending balance, add deposits the bank has not recorded yet ("deposits in transit"), and subtract checks and payments that have not cleared ("outstanding"). The result should equal your register balance.

misconceptions.B: Uses the statement balance without adjusting
misconceptions.A: Subtracts the deposit and the checks

questions.prompt: Sam reconciles his account. After he adds deposits in transit and subtracts outstanding checks, the statement shows $565, but his register shows $575. Which is the most likely explanation?

choices.text: The bank always makes small $10 errors in its own favor
Sam's deposit in transit was $10 smaller than he thought
Interest earned is never shown on statements
A $10 charge on the statement was never recorded in his register

questions.correct_answer: A $10 charge on the statement was never recorded in his register
questions.intro: When the adjusted statement balance and the register do not match, look for items on the statement that are missing from the register, such as fees, interest, or automatic payments, and for math mistakes in the register.
questions.feedback: A $10 fee or charge that Sam did not record would make his register $10 too high.

misconceptions.B: Would make the adjusted balance lower, not his register higher

questions.prompt: Sam finds a $4 monthly "service fee" on his statement that he did not record. What should he do in his register?

choices.text: Subtract $4 from his register balance
Add $4 to his register balance
Ignore it, since the bank already recorded it
Subtract $8, once for the bank and once for him

questions.feedback: A fee is money out, so Sam subtracts $4 to keep his register correct.

misconceptions.C: Thinks only one record needs updating

questions.prompt: Which reason BEST explains why reconciling monthly matters?

choices.text: It raises the interest rate on the account
It is legally required for every account holder
It removes any fees the bank charged that month
It catches errors and unauthorized charges early

questions.correct_answer: It catches errors and unauthorized charges early
questions.feedback: Spotting problems early matters because reporting deadlines apply to unauthorized transfers and errors.

No: her register should show $375
Yes, because the two numbers are close

questions.prompt: Lucas sees a $129 charge from an online store he has never used. What should he do FIRST?

choices.text: Wait until next month to see if it happens again
Email the online store his full account number to ask about the charge
Ignore it, because small banks cannot reverse charges
Contact his bank right away to report the unauthorized charge

questions.correct_answer: Contact his bank right away to report the unauthorized charge
questions.intro: An unauthorized transaction is one you did not make or allow. Federal rules (Regulation E) limit your liability for unauthorized electronic transfers, but the protection depends on how fast you report. Contact your bank as soon as you notice one.
questions.feedback: Reporting quickly keeps his liability limits as low as possible.

misconceptions.B: Shares sensitive data with an unknown party

questions.prompt: Mia's statement dated March 31 shows an unauthorized online debit charge; her card was never lost or stolen. She reports it on May 20. Is she within the window for full protection?

choices.text: Yes; it is within 60 days of the statement
No; the limit is 2 business days
No; charges must be reported the same day they post
Yes, because there is no time limit at all

questions.correct_answer: Yes; it is within 60 days of the statement
questions.intro: For unauthorized electronic transfers that appear on a statement, you generally have 60 days after the statement is sent to report them. After that, you may be liable for later transfers the bank could have stopped.
questions.feedback: March 31 to May 20 is 50 days, inside the 60-day window. If a card is lost or stolen, report within 2 business days of learning of it for the lowest limit ($50).

questions.prompt: A store charged Ana twice for one $45 purchase. Which statement is accurate?

choices.text: Duplicate charges are legal if the store says so
She must accept it because she used her card
She can only fix it by closing her account
This is an error she can dispute with the bank or the store

questions.correct_answer: This is an error she can dispute with the bank or the store
questions.feedback: A duplicate charge is an error. She can ask the store for a refund and dispute it with her bank.

misconceptions.B: Thinks using the card waives rights
misconceptions.C: Thinks closing the account is the only fix

choices.text: Transaction alerts and frequent app checks
Reading paper statements once a year
Checking only the ending balance on each statement
Using the card less often

questions.correct_answer: Transaction alerts and frequent app checks
questions.feedback: Alerts and frequent checks spot problems within days.

questions.prompt: Ben lost his debit card on Monday, noticed it Tuesday, and reported it Tuesday. A thief spent $300 before he reported it. What is the most Ben can be held responsible for under federal rules?

choices.text: $0, in every case

questions.intro: For a lost or stolen debit card, if you report within 2 business days of learning of the loss, your liability for unauthorized transfers is capped at $50. After 2 business days, the cap rises to $500. Many banks voluntarily offer $0 liability, but the law sets these limits.
questions.feedback: He reported within 2 business days of learning of the loss, so the legal cap is $50.

misconceptions.A: Thinks he owes everything the thief spent
misconceptions.B: Uses the limit for late reports
misconceptions.C: Assumes there is never any liability
